paragraphs: Understanding how all input features jointly affect a prediction can be difficult when data are high dimensional and labeled examples are scarce. This paper takes a more focused approach: comparing the influence of two features on the response. It introduces a definition of closeness of influence that recovers the familiar comparison of coefficient magnitudes in parametric models.

The authors then develop a statistical test for this comparison without requiring a particular model for the relationship between inputs and responses. Its finite-sample guarantee controls the type I error rate regardless of the true conditional distribution of the response. This separates the validity of the test from assumptions about a specific prediction model.

The paper also studies when the test can reliably detect differences. For linear regression and binary classification under Gaussian mixture models, an appropriate internal score function and sufficiently many samples yield full statistical power. Numerical experiments include a CIFAR-10 datamodel application that identifies training examples with different influences on a trained model.
icml-2023-a-model-free-closeness-of-infl.tldr: The paper introduces a model-free test for comparing two features’ influence, with finite-sample error control and conditional power guarantees.

paragraphs: Diffusion models generate samples by learning to reverse a process that gradually turns data into noise. Their practical success leaves theoretical questions about why some design choices matter more than others. This paper focuses on their relatively weak sensitivity to the chosen noise family and the importance of scheduling noise levels appropriately.

The authors connect diffusion to serial reproduction, a cognitive science paradigm in which people repeatedly observe stimuli and reproduce them from memory. They identify a correspondence between this repeated reconstruction process and diffusion models. Through that connection, the two properties become understandable consequences of a shared structure, rather than isolated observations about generative modeling.

Simulations complement the theoretical analysis by exhibiting the same key features. The contribution is an explanation of observed behavior through a connection to an established cognitive paradigm. It clarifies why noise-family choice can have limited influence while the progression of noise levels remains consequential for synthesis, without claiming that every noise choice or schedule works equally well.
icml-2023-analyzing-diffusion-as-serial-.tldr: A connection to serial reproduction in cognitive science explains diffusion models’ weak sensitivity to noise families and their need for suitable noise schedules.

paragraphs: This paper studies a bandit learner that receives rewards through a noisy communication channel. A client encodes the reward from each chosen action, subject to a bound on the encoded signal’s second moment. Gaussian noise then corrupts that signal, so the learner must discover good actions using feedback that is both communication constrained and noisy.

The authors derive a lower bound on the worst-case regret achievable by any method. It grows with the square root of the number of actions times the time horizon, with an additional penalty when the signal-to-noise ratio is below one. This quantifies how communication quality limits decision-making performance.

Their proposed algorithm, UE-UCB++, approaches this lower bound up to a minor additive term. It starts with phases of uniform exploration and finishes with upper-confidence-bound action selection. Crucially, rough reward estimates from one exploration phase improve the encoding protocol for the next. Better encoding then produces more accurate estimates, reducing the amount of uniform exploration needed before exploiting promising actions.
icml-2023-communication-constrained-band.tldr: An adaptive reward-encoding bandit algorithm nearly matches the fundamental regret limit imposed by communication constraints and Gaussian noise.

paragraphs: This paper examines a computational imbalance between attacking a classifier and making it robust. For ReLU classifiers, the authors prove that finding attacks is NP-hard, while ensuring robustness during training is hard for a higher level of the polynomial hierarchy, even for a single example. The result provides a complexity-based rationale for why robustness methods can still be defeated.

The authors then show that this particular imbalance does not carry over to all inference-time certification methods. Their proof-of-concept defense, Counter-Attack, reverses the direction: running the defense is NP-hard, while attacking it is hard for the higher complexity class. These are computational hardness statements, rather than claims that the defense is inexpensive to run.

Motivated by this reversal, the paper explores using adversarial attacks as components of robustness certification and evaluates their effectiveness empirically. It also releases the UG100 attack benchmark. Together, the contributions distinguish the computational demands of robust training from those of certification and show how attack procedures can contribute to a defensive objective.
icml-2023-computational-asymmetries-in-r.tldr: The paper proves computational asymmetries between attack and defense and introduces an inference-time certification approach that reverses their direction.

paragraphs: Classification systems often minimize cross-entropy even though their ultimate goal is to avoid incorrect predictions. This paper studies how improvement in such a training loss translates into improvement in classification error. Its analysis covers a broader family called comp-sum losses, including cross-entropy, generalized cross-entropy, and mean absolute error.

The authors establish tight, non-asymptotic H-consistency bounds that connect surrogate-loss estimation error to zero-one-loss estimation error within the chosen hypothesis set. Accounting for that set matters because the guarantee concerns the models actually available to the learner. The bounds involve minimizability gaps, which the paper analyzes specifically for comp-sum losses to make the guarantees more explicit.

The paper also introduces smooth adversarial versions of these losses and proves corresponding H-consistency guarantees. Minimizing regularized forms produces new adversarial robustness algorithms. Alongside the theory, experiments compare the loss family and report that the proposed robustness algorithms outperform the evaluated state of the art while also improving ordinary, non-adversarial accuracy. Those performance gains are experimental findings, distinct from the theoretical bounds.
icml-2023-cross-entropy-loss-functions-t.tldr: Tight guarantees connect cross-entropy-like training losses to classification error and motivate new losses with reported adversarial robustness gains.

paragraphs: Gaussian-process classification becomes computationally demanding when a problem has many classes. This paper introduces Efficient Transformed Gaussian Processes, or ETGP, to construct multiple dependent processes while keeping the number of Gaussian-process operations independent of the number of processes. That targets expensive operations such as inverting an inducing-point covariance matrix.

ETGP starts from a single Gaussian-process sample and applies a separate invertible transformation for each process. This construction makes the processes dependent without a mixing matrix and allows them to be non-stationary, meaning their behavior need not be uniform across the input space. The shared starting point is central to combining expressive class relationships with computational efficiency.

The authors derive a sparse variational inference algorithm and evaluate the method on five classification tasks, ranging in dataset size and from a few classes to hundreds. ETGP generally outperforms the compared leading Gaussian-process classifiers and has roughly an order of magnitude lower computational cost. The efficiency claim specifically concerns Gaussian-process operations; it does not assert that every part of computation is independent of class count.
icml-2023-efficient-transformed-gaussian.tldr: ETGP creates dependent, non-stationary class processes from one Gaussian process, reducing computation while generally improving classification in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Denoising methods can be trained without clean reference images, yet evaluating them often still depends on having those references. This creates a practical mismatch: strong performance on synthetic-noise benchmarks does not supply a way to assess a method where only noisy observations exist. The paper addresses this evaluation problem directly.

The authors introduce unsupervised versions of mean squared error and peak signal-to-noise ratio that use noisy data alone. Their theoretical analysis establishes asymptotic consistency: the proposed quantities approach their supervised counterparts in the relevant large-sample limit. This supports their use as estimators of familiar quality measures, rather than treating them as unrelated proxies.

Controlled experiments with synthetic noise show accurate approximations in practice. The authors also validate the approach on raw-format video and transmission electron microscopy data, covering two real imaging modalities. The stated result is that denoising methods can be evaluated using exclusively noisy observations. The asymptotic guarantee and empirical checks play complementary roles: one establishes limiting behavior, while the other demonstrates usefulness in the examined finite-data settings.
icml-2023-evaluating-unsupervised-denois.tldr: Two noisy-data-only metrics estimate conventional denoising quality measures, with asymptotic guarantees and validation on synthetic and real imaging data.

paragraphs: Many scientific and engineering optimization problems involve expensive evaluations over large search spaces. This paper considers access to a fixed dataset for pretraining and only a small budget for new evaluations. It identifies a weakness in approaches that learn the objective function or its inverse: their predictions can be insufficiently accurate away from the offline data distribution.

BONET instead trains a generative model on sequences derived from the available dataset. Its sampling procedure constructs fixed-length trajectories with monotonic transitions from lower-fidelity to higher-fidelity samples. An autoregressive model learns these trajectories, turning the offline examples into training material for an optimizer that generates sequences.

The empirical implementation uses a causally masked Transformer and is evaluated on Design-Bench. BONET achieves the best average ranking and outperforms the compared state-of-the-art baselines. The significance is that generative pretraining can learn an optimization procedure from existing data, rather than relying solely on an accurate function approximation throughout the search space. The reported advantage is an average benchmark result, not a claim of superiority on every optimization problem.
icml-2023-generative-pretraining-for-bla.tldr: BONET learns an optimizer by generatively pretraining on trajectories constructed from offline data and achieves the best average ranking on Design-Bench.

paragraphs: Ranking models are often trained with a convenient surrogate loss instead of the loss that directly measures incorrect ordering. This paper asks whether reducing surrogate error guarantees a reduction in ranking error within a particular model family. H-consistency bounds formalize that connection by bounding target-loss estimation error using surrogate-loss estimation error.

The authors find a substantial obstruction in both general pairwise ranking and bipartite ranking. For most practical hypothesis sets covered by their equicontinuity condition, including linear models and neural networks, meaningful bounds of this kind do not exist. The result concerns a specific theoretical guarantee and the model classes satisfying the stated property.

The proposed response is to allow abstention: a ranker may decline to make a prediction at a limited cost. For surrogate losses corresponding to these abstention objectives, the paper derives H-consistency bounds for linear functions and neural networks with one hidden layer. Experiments illustrate the effectiveness of ranking with abstention. Allowing a paid refusal therefore changes the ranking objective in a way that makes useful theoretical guarantees possible.
icml-2023-h-consistency-bounds-for-pairw.tldr: Allowing ranking models to abstain at a cost enables H-consistency guarantees where common ranking objectives lack meaningful bounds for many practical model classes.

paragraphs: Resource-allocation policies decide how to distribute a limited supply of interventions. Evaluating them through randomized trials is difficult because resource constraints link participants’ outcomes through the policy’s decisions. Increasing the trial size alone does not remove this interdependence, so conventional comparisons of experimental-arm averages leave an important estimation challenge.

The paper introduces an estimator based on retrospectively reshuffling participants between trial arms. The authors identify conditions under which these reassignments are permissible and the outcomes of the resulting counterfactual trials can be determined accurately without running new experiments. The reshuffling is therefore a way to extract additional information from an already completed trial.

Theoretical results show that the estimator remains unbiased while reducing variance compared with common sample-mean estimators. Experiments using synthetic data, semisynthetic data, and real case-study data report improved estimation accuracy throughout. The key qualification is that the counterfactual reassignments must satisfy the identified conditions; arbitrary reshuffling is not justified. Within that framework, the method improves policy evaluation by reusing the structure of existing trial evidence.
icml-2023-improved-policy-evaluation-for.tldr: Permissible retrospective participant reshuffling yields an unbiased, lower-variance estimator for randomized trials of resource-allocation policies.

paragraphs: Estimating covariance matrices can be expensive when each sample requires a costly simulation or measurement. This paper combines data sources with different costs and levels of fidelity, using their shared information to reduce estimation variance. Its central concern is to gain that efficiency while preserving positive definiteness, a structural property needed by downstream methods.

The proposed estimator works with the log-Euclidean geometry of symmetric positive-definite matrices. This geometric formulation guarantees definiteness when combining information across the hierarchy of sources, addressing a weakness of previous approaches. The authors also develop an optimal allocation of samples across sources to minimize mean squared error under a fixed budget.

Evaluations use physical application data from heat conduction and fluid dynamics. The reported outcomes include more accurate metric learning and speedups exceeding an order of magnitude relative to the benchmarks. These findings connect the estimator’s mathematical structure to practical value: cheaper sources can help reduce sampling costs while the resulting covariance estimate retains a property crucial for metric learning, data assimilation, and related tasks.
icml-2023-multi-fidelity-covariance-esti.tldr: A geometry-aware covariance estimator combines sources of different costs while guaranteeing positive definiteness and optimally allocating a fixed sampling budget.

paragraphs: Neural networks can approximate solutions of high-dimensional partial differential equations, raising the question of when their size can avoid exponential growth with dimension. Much existing theory addresses linear equations. This paper extends the representational analysis to nonlinear elliptic variational equations, whose solutions minimize a specified energy functional.

The main result is conditional on how composition with derivatives of that energy’s integrand affects Barron norm, a measure used to control neural approximation complexity. Under the stated growth condition, the authors bound the Barron norm needed to approximate the solution in L2. That bound translates into a size bound for a two-layer neural network. With approximation accuracy and the relevant growth parameters fixed, the size grows polynomially with dimension.

The proof simulates a preconditioned gradient procedure in a suitable Hilbert space. The procedure converges exponentially fast, while the analysis tracks Barron-norm growth at each step. This establishes representational guarantees for the covered nonlinear equations and substantially generalizes related linear results. The escape from dimensionality depends on the stated composition condition and fixed-parameter interpretation.
icml-2023-neural-network-approximations-.tldr: Under a Barron-norm growth condition, certain nonlinear PDE solutions admit two-layer neural approximations whose size is polynomial in dimension for fixed accuracy and parameters.

paragraphs: This paper studies models that learn a sequence of tasks requiring both perception and symbolic reasoning. Each task maps low-level inputs to concepts and uses prior knowledge to produce predictions. A useful feature of this setting is that different tasks often share concepts whose meanings remain stable, even as the tasks themselves change.

Simply combining existing approaches does not fully solve the problem. Standard continual-learning strategies ignore knowledge, while ordinary neuro-symbolic models can forget earlier tasks. Combining the two helps with forgetting but can introduce reasoning shortcuts: predictions may fit the reasoning structure while the learned concepts acquire the wrong meanings. The authors show that detailed prior knowledge and exact inference do not by themselves prevent this failure.

The proposed strategy, COOL, focuses continual learning at the concept level so that useful concept meanings are acquired and retained. On three new benchmarks, it sustains high performance on tasks where other strategies fail. The findings make concept quality a central part of continual learning: preserving predictive behavior alone can leave the underlying concepts unsuitable for later tasks.
icml-2023-neuro-symbolic-continual-learn.tldr: COOL preserves concept meanings across neuro-symbolic tasks, addressing both forgetting and reasoning shortcuts that can survive exact inference.

paragraphs: This paper asks how accurately a changing probability distribution can be estimated from a sequence of independent observations. The observations come from distributions that gradually evolve over time, while the target is the current distribution. That distinction matters: the available evidence spans different distributions rather than repeated draws from one unchanging source.

The authors establish tight minimax risk bounds for two settings: discrete distributions and continuous distributions with smooth densities. Minimax analysis considers the best possible estimator against the most difficult distribution allowed by the drift constraints. Tight bounds therefore characterize the achievable worst-case accuracy, rather than reporting only the performance of one particular estimation procedure.

The analysis handles a broad class of drift models and extends earlier results on agnostic learning with drift. Its contribution is a theoretical account of what can be learned when the data-generating distribution moves over time. The conclusions remain tied to the specified drift constraints, and smoothness enters the continuous-density setting. Together, these conditions define the changing distributions over which the accuracy guarantees are established.
icml-2023-nonparametric-density-estimati.tldr: The paper establishes tight worst-case accuracy bounds for estimating current discrete and smooth continuous distributions from independent data collected under drift.

paragraphs: Many causal inference methods summarize an intervention through an average potential outcome or an average treatment effect. Such summaries leave out the rest of the outcome distribution. This paper instead estimates the density of potential outcomes after an intervention using observational data, targeting a fuller description of what outcomes an intervention could produce.

The proposed Interventional Normalizing Flows combine two flow models with distinct roles. A nuisance flow estimates supporting quantities, while a target flow provides a parametric model of the outcome density. The authors derive a tractable training objective using a one-step bias correction, designed for efficient and doubly robust estimation of the target parameters.

The resulting density is properly normalized, so the model supplies a probability density rather than an unnormalized score. Across the reported experiments, the method is expressive, effective, and scales well with sample size and high-dimensional confounding. The authors position it as, to their knowledge, the first proper fully parametric deep-learning approach for this density-estimation task. Its main advance is bringing flexible distribution modeling into the estimation of intervention outcomes.
icml-2023-normalizing-flows-for-interven.tldr: Interventional Normalizing Flows combine nuisance and target density models with bias correction to estimate full potential-outcome distributions from observational data.

paragraphs: A generative model aims to represent a data distribution, so its generalization analysis needs to address distributional agreement beyond the training sample. This paper extends PAC-Bayesian theory to that setting. It develops guarantees based on Wasserstein distance and total variation distance, providing two ways to quantify differences between generated and target distributions.

The Wasserstein results use two distinct routes. The first assumes a bounded instance space, while the second takes advantage of dimensionality reduction. These details matter because they specify how the authors obtain the guarantees. The results apply naturally to Wasserstein GANs and Energy-Based GANs, and the resulting bounds also suggest new objectives for training these models.

Although the contribution is mainly theoretical, numerical experiments on synthetic datasets produce non-vacuous bounds for Wasserstein GANs. This means the reported guarantees provide meaningful information in those experiments rather than being too loose to be useful. The work therefore connects a generalization framework to both model optimization and concrete numerical certification, with the empirical evidence specifically supplied for the synthetic Wasserstein-GAN setting.
icml-2023-pac-bayesian-generalization-bo.tldr: PAC-Bayesian bounds for distributional distances yield new generative-model training objectives and non-vacuous Wasserstein-GAN guarantees on synthetic data.

paragraphs: Fully sharded data-parallel training helps distribute large neural models, but communication can still limit scaling. Much of that communication carries model weights, making compression especially delicate: directly quantizing those weights can change training convergence and reduce accuracy. This paper introduces QSDP to support compression of both weights and gradients with theoretical guarantees.

The underlying result shows that a modified stochastic gradient method can converge while maintaining only quantized weights. This is significant because training then takes place over a highly non-convex collection of quantized points. QSDP builds on that result to provide a variant of fully sharded training that the authors describe as simple to implement with essentially no overhead.

The evaluation trains GPT-family models with as many as 1.3 billion parameters across multiple cluster nodes. In these experiments, QSDP preserves model accuracy, removes the observed communication bottlenecks of fully sharded training, and achieves end-to-end speedups of up to 2.2 times. The result connects a convergence argument for quantized optimization to measured improvements in distributed large-model training.
icml-2023-quantized-distributed-training.tldr: QSDP quantizes weights and gradients with convergence guarantees, preserving accuracy and delivering up to 2.2-fold training speedups in the reported GPT experiments.

paragraphs: Probabilistic forecasts describe distributions of possible outcomes, and proper scoring rules are commonly used to evaluate them. A proper rule favors the true distribution in expectation. This paper shows why that desirable property does not by itself ensure that an evaluation with a finite amount of data can distinguish forecasting errors reliably.

The authors conduct a systematic finite-sample study using statistical power analysis. For each scoring rule, they identify a region of reliability: practical conditions under which the rule can be trusted to detect discrepancies between a forecast distribution and the truth. This shifts attention from an ideal expectation-based property to the actual ability of an evaluation to reveal mistakes.

The analysis uses a synthetic benchmark designed around several important distributional discrepancies. An electricity-production application then examines how the findings carry over to a real task. The results expose substantial shortcomings in commonly used evaluations of multivariate probabilistic forecasts. Their implication is that a scoring rule’s theoretical propriety and its practical error-detection ability need to be assessed separately.
icml-2023-regions-of-reliability-in-the-.tldr: Finite-sample power analysis reveals when proper scoring rules can reliably detect errors in multivariate probabilistic forecasts.

paragraphs: The geometry of a language model’s latent representations can help explain how it uses its available representational space. This paper focuses on data spread: how fully representations occupy that space. Reliable measurement matters if researchers want to compare models or manipulate geometric properties in pursuit of better downstream performance.

The authors demonstrate that two commonly used measures, average cosine similarity and a partition-function minimum-to-maximum ratio, do not reliably compare space usage across different data distributions. They propose six alternative measures and examine them on seven synthetic distributions. All six improve on the existing measures in that evaluation, showing that familiar summaries can miss aspects of spread that alternative measurements capture.

From these alternatives, the paper recommends one measure based on principal components and another based on entropy. Both provide reliable relative comparisons and support comparisons across models of different sizes and representation dimensions. The contribution is a better basis for measuring latent geometry; the stated experiments establish comparative measurement behavior rather than a downstream performance gain from changing a model’s representations.
icml-2023-reliable-measures-of-spread-in.tldr: The paper identifies unreliable latent-space spread metrics and recommends principal-component and entropy-based alternatives for comparing different models.

paragraphs: Antibody design requires new sequences that are diverse while remaining structurally consistent. The complementarity-determining region is especially important because it influences binding affinity and specificity. Limited antibody sequence-and-structure data can constrain deep-learning methods, particularly their ability to generate a diverse collection of candidate sequences.

ReprogBert addresses this data constraint by repurposing a pretrained English language model for protein sequence infilling. The approach uses model reprogramming to adapt knowledge from a source language to a different sequence domain with scarce task data. Its central idea is to make an existing language model useful for filling antibody sequence regions when learning an effective model from the available antibody data is difficult.

On antibody-design benchmarks with limited sequence data, the model produces CDR sequences with diversity gains exceeding twofold over baselines in the reported results, while retaining structural integrity and naturalness. The generated sequences also show enhanced antigen-binding specificity and virus-neutralization ability. These findings support cross-language model adaptation as a useful approach to the examined antibody-design setting, with gains extending beyond diversity alone.
icml-2023-reprogramming-pretrained-langu.tldr: ReprogBert repurposes an English language model for antibody infilling, reporting greater sequence diversity while retaining structural quality and improving functional properties.

paragraphs: Computer-vision networks can make unreliable predictions when images contain adversarial perturbations. This paper introduces a framework that enforces constraints during inference, allowing the model to adjust to the particular image being processed. The approach places part of the robustness effort at testing time, where an image’s distinctive or unfamiliar characteristics are available.

The authors argue theoretically for using many constraints at inference rather than relying on a single one. Their method uses feature equivariance, which supplies fine-grained relationships in the feature space that can serve as dense constraints. Restoring those relationships provides the mechanism for making inference more robust on each input.

Experiments show that restoring feature equivariance defends against the evaluated worst-case adversarial perturbations. The reported improvements span ImageNet, Cityscapes, PASCAL VOC, and MS-COCO, covering image recognition, semantic segmentation, and instance segmentation. This breadth supports the usefulness of the inference-time framework across the examined visual tasks. The theoretical emphasis on dense constraints and the empirical robustness results together motivate equivariance as a practical source of image-specific corrective information.
icml-2023-robust-perception-through-equi.tldr: Enforcing dense feature-equivariance constraints at inference improves adversarial robustness across several recognition and segmentation benchmarks.

paragraphs: Multimodal models learn from heterogeneous inputs such as video, audio, and text. Deployment can change which input types are available, especially across hardware platforms. This paper studies that mismatch between training and deployment, asking how well learned representations continue to work when the available modalities differ.

The authors introduce a robustness framework for systematically analyzing common multimodal representation-learning methods. Using it, they identify weaknesses in existing approaches and propose two interventions. The framework makes changing modality availability an explicit evaluation concern, so that a model’s use of several inputs can be assessed alongside its ability to cope with a different input combination.

Experiments on AudioSet, Kinetics-400, and ImageNet-Captions report robustness improvements ranging from 1.5 to 4 times. The interventions also make better use of additional modalities when they are available, achieving a competitive 44.2 mean average precision on AudioSet 20K. The findings therefore address two related deployment needs: maintaining performance under modality mismatch and benefiting from richer inputs when a platform can supply them.
icml-2023-robustness-in-multimodal-learn.tldr: A modality-mismatch evaluation framework motivates two interventions that improve reported robustness and make better use of additional inputs.

paragraphs: This paper investigates privacy in federated learning with FedAvg, a central server, and a model whose first layer is fully connected. Even when secure aggregation is used, the server receives aggregated models. SRATTA examines what sensitive information can be recovered from those aggregate outputs alone under the paper’s stated realistic assumptions.

The attack does two things: it reconstructs client data samples and groups recovered samples according to which client supplied them. The second capability is the distinctive contribution. Recovering isolated examples already threatens privacy, but linking examples to a shared client reveals additional structure despite aggregation hiding individual contributions.

The authors provide theoretical grounding and demonstrate practical use on realistic models and datasets. They describe the result as a significant threat to the privacy protection expected from secure aggregation in this setting. They also propose countermeasures and argue that clients should actively participate in protecting privacy during training. The finding is tied to the specified model architecture, training setup, and attack assumptions, while showing that aggregate-only access can still support both recovery and attribution.
icml-2023-sratta-sample-re-attribution-a.tldr: Under the studied FedAvg assumptions, SRATTA recovers samples and groups them by client using only aggregated models, exposing a privacy risk despite secure aggregation.

paragraphs: The stochastic gradient bandit algorithm is an established method for learning which actions give better rewards. This paper supplies a global convergence result that had remained unproven: the algorithm approaches an optimal policy at an O(1/t) rate even with a constant step size. The analysis explains how its own updates provide enough noise regulation and exploration.

The first key finding is a growth condition on update noise. Its variance shrinks when progress becomes small, so decreasing the step size is unnecessary for the stated convergence result. The second finding concerns action probabilities: stochastic updates prevent them from decaying faster than O(1/t), ensuring that every action is sampled infinitely often with probability one.

Together, these properties explain how exploration and exploitation remain balanced sufficiently for almost-sure convergence to a global optimum. Continued sampling prevents actions from being permanently neglected, while diminishing update variance supports convergence without an externally shrinking step size. Experiments further verify the theoretical findings. The contribution concerns the analyzed bandit algorithm and establishes why its existing stochastic update mechanism can suffice.
icml-2023-stochastic-gradient-succeeds-f.tldr: The stochastic gradient bandit algorithm converges globally at O(1/t) with a constant step size because its updates provide sufficient exploration and shrinking noise.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning must improve a policy using an existing dataset, making unsupported decisions vulnerable to extrapolation error. Many methods address this by keeping the learned policy’s action probabilities close to those of the behavior policy that generated the data. This paper argues that matching those probabilities can constrain learning too strongly.

Supported Trust Region optimization, or STR, instead constrains the policy to the behavior policy’s support. The policy remains within the actions covered by that support while gaining more freedom to change their probabilities. STR combines this less restrictive condition with trust-region policy optimization, seeking improvement without requiring close agreement with the behavior policy’s density.

When approximation and sampling errors are absent, the authors prove strict improvement until convergence to the optimal policy within the dataset’s support constraint. Their analysis also provides safe stepwise improvement guarantees with both errors incorporated. Experiments on MuJoCo locomotion and the more challenging AntMaze domains support the theory and report state-of-the-art performance. The optimality claim is explicitly support constrained, rather than unrestricted over all possible policies.
icml-2023-supported-trust-region-optimiz.tldr: STR improves offline policies within behavior-policy support, providing improvement guarantees and strong reported performance with a less restrictive policy constraint.
